newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian pineapple sector fights for survival.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian pineapple sector fights for survival.

text.p: Ivory Coast's pineapple sector, squeezed by falling prices and stiff competition from Central America, has cut freight rates in what is beginning to look like a fight for survival.
Confronted by aggressively-priced rates on its own doorstep, producer group OCAB on Friday cut its rate for fresh pineapples to Europe from $107 a palette to $89 for the rest of 1996.

But the new rate is still $13 higher than on a boat chartered by competitors operating out of Cameroon, leading to accusations that rivals -- particularly U.S. giant Dole Food Co Inc -- are trying to knock Ivory Coast out of the market.

OCAB President Matthias N'Goan denounced what he called "the selfish visions of an American company, which, through a French company, seems to have one aim -- to keep the pineapple sector in a state of permanent stagnation."

A statement issued after a three-day meeting of pineapple producers and importers highlighted what it called "attempts by a Franco-American company to break the (market) balance secured at the cost of great sacrifices" by everyone in the sector.
OCAB, which charters its own ships, said this year's marketing campaign was marked by a "collapse of prices on the different European markets".
Having invested in improving the quality of their product, Ivorian producers have watched prices in Europe crumble -- from 4.1 French Francs (FF) a kilo in 1993 to 3.35 FF in August 1996.

"Since June, we are faced with overproduction of fruit in Europe... as a result, prices are very, very low," Xavier Espana, president of the European Association of Pineapple Importers of Ivory Coast (ASEIMPAC) told the meeting.
Strikes in France, the main destination for Ivorian pineapples, during the high season in December made matters worse.

OCAB and ASEIMPAC, who control 95 percent of Ivory Coast pineapple production, joined forces in 1992 and many of their members accuse Dole of trying to break up the united front that has enabled them to build up the sector.
"The two organisations recall the divisions which from 1986 almost ruined the sector and which were nothing more than Ivorians competing against one another," their statement said.
Dole has no direct presence in the region but OCAB members accuse it of using Compagnie Fruitiere de France, in which it has a stake, to destabilise the market.
The French company chartered a boat from Cameroon which left Abidjan on Tuesday shipping pineapples at $76 a palette.

Two local companies -- Marexport and Siga -- broke ranks and took advantage of the cheap rates. Marexport, industry sources say, is controlled by Sofipa, which is in turn controlled by Compagnie Fruitiere de France.
Ivorian banana growers also face a slump in prices, compounded by a flood of cheap fruit from Central and Latin America. Banana prices have fallen from six FF in 1990 to 3.50 FF in 1996.

Ivory Coast exported 155,000 tonnes of pineapples and 200,000 tonnes of bananas in the crop year from October 1995 to September 1996, up from around 145,000 tonnes and 170,000 tonnes respectively in the previous crop year.
OCAB says that in the fresh mango sector, things are looking up, largely thanks to its shipping arrangements which have opened up the European market.
Exports in the 1996 season -- March-July -- fell from 7,500 tonnes to just under 6,000 tonnes but this was due to a fall in output based on less favourable weather conditions.
($1=5.1 French Francs)
